#2796. Cowboys HC Brian Schottenheimer can’t shift the blame forever

When Brian Schottenheimer was announced as the Dallas Cowboys head coach, most fans and people around the football world were not very excited with the hire.

After hearing him speak, many got on board with giving him a chance. In year one, the Cowboys offense showed some positive signs of improvement, but historically bad defensive results resulted in the team missing the playoffs and finishing the season with a disappointing 7-9-1 record.

Over the offseason, the Cowboys fired long-time defensive coordinator Matt Eberflus and elected to hire Christian Parker. That decision was met with plenty of praise around league circles and the expectations that the defense would make some major improvements in 2026.

As we know now, that was not the case and this season is feeling eerily similar to 2025. With Eberflus fired and Christian Parker now stripped of his play-calling duties, head coach Brian Schottenheimer is running out of people to blame for his own shortcomings.

It's widely known that Eberflus was more of a front office hire given his familiarity with the Jones', his veteran experience as a defensive coordinator, and his recent experience as a head coach to support first-time head coach Brian Schottenheimer.

After that did not work out, Schottenheimer almost bragged up his process in landing Christian Parker and talked plenty this offseason about how the 2026 Dallas Cowboys had a "championship roster" coming into the season. With Matt Eberflus' unit being blamed for the 2025 Cowboys struggles, Christian Parker is now taking the blame for the 2026 Cowboys struggles.

Like most teams, the Cowboys have dealt with their fair-share of injuries on the defensive side of the ball, but most of their key players on defense have remained healthy this season. The defensive results in 2026 have just about matched the results the defense had in 2025, and even performing worse by some metrics.

Even with the defense being the main cause of their struggles in 2026, Brian Schottenheimer's inconsistency as a play-caller on offense and in-game management blunders have been just as detrimental to the team's success.

Schottenheimer was able to win a lot of people over with his words in press conferences and radio hits, but given how his first two seasons as a head coach have gone, the time for talk is over. The Cowboys need results and so far the team's 11-15-1 record with a healthy Dak Prescott is simply not good enough. Schottenheimer's last ditch effort move to name Mike Pettine the defensive play-caller may work, or it may not, but currently it feels like a panic move to help take some of the heat off himself.

We have just seven weeks left of the regular season to figure out if it was the right move or not. If it is, and the Cowboys somehow make the playoffs, expect to see Schottenheimer back in 2027. If it doesn't, it's hard to imagine the Jones' will have belief in the head coach's ability to win the NFC East given the state the division is in this year.

#2789. Pistons vs Raptors preview: 2nd NBA Cup game

Early season Fridays = NBA Cup day! The Detroit Pistons can climb to 2-0 in group play with a win over the worse-than-expected Toronto Raptors (1-1 in group play). The NBA thought this would've been a big game, handing out the Prime Video first game slot, but injuries, injuries, injuries.

Ron Holland, Duncan Robinson, and Jalen Duren are out again, but Cade Cunningham is expected to play. Injuries have slowed down the Raptors a ton.

RJ Barrett and Collin Murray-Boyles won't suit up in Detroit. Kawhi Leonard remains out. His absence is the main source of Toronto's struggle, but I still expected more.

The Raptors are still live even though they should be better. That said, Detroit isn't a team that takes opponents lightly because of who's in or out. The Pistons play the same brand of ball regardless of who's out there on either side.

Wednesday's 122-109 win over the New Orleans Pelicans tripled down on that point. Even a shorthanded Pistons squad without Cade manages to find a way.

Daniss Jenkins. Javonte Green. Ausar Thompson with the ball. Paul Reed with extended minutes — trustworthy things.

We got Isaiah Joe back in the lineup in that one! One of the marquee signings of Detroit's offseason let it fly. Joe went 3-for-5 from range and put it on the floor, aiding Detroit's flow. Bball Paul said Joe had more in his game during media day. Paul knows ball.

The ability to leverage your shooting with live dribble decisions is an invaluable skill come playoff time. Love seeing Joe back out there, and more of that would be cool.

John Collins was on a heater (4-6 on 3s). He should get six 3s up every night with the room he has to fire. Collins will be matched up with Jakob Poeltl tonight. Poeltl is arguably the biggest hacker in the league. His 5.6 foul percentage ranks in the fourth percentile among bigs.

A lot of those Cade drives should end with trips to the charity stripe. Cade's .37 FTr is a career high. He's getting the calls and shooting ~86 percent at the line. That works. Cade is also putting together a strong All-Defense case, being a big-time contributor on the sixth-best defense.

Per Stathead, only Cade, Nikola Jokić, Matisse Thybulle, Scottie Barnes, and Caleb Wilson are averaging at least 0.9 blocks and 1.4 steals. Cade is doing this without fouling. He's leveling up even more on that end.

Barnes recently declared himself the best defender in the world. I have no problem with that. He is up there. He's a legit 1-5 defender. Anybody that good at something should feel they're the best. That confidence got them where they are.

Barnes is Barnes, but I thought Toronto would have a more intimidating team defense. Cleaning The Glass ranks them 17th overall and 19th over the past two weeks + they are on a six-game losing streak.

The injury bug cannot be ignored, but I thought Toronto would be immune to long stretches of defensive lapses because of their suffocating gap principles.

Those principles still force turnovers at a frightening rate (2nd), but they haven't dug in and clamped down like last year's Raptors team. They're still feisty enough to muddy up a game, but I expected more.

Toronto's off-the-bounce creation takes a big blow with no Kawhi and Barrett. Barnes has more shot-making responsibilities this season. His 23.8 points per game are a career high. Immanuel Quickley will get them up. Catching fire vs. Ausar and the Pistons' defense isn't easy, but Toronto is looking to Quickley to provide immediate offense.

Jamison Battle is one of Toronto's consistent snipers. He's not a shooter you can disregard and is coming off a 19-point, 5-for-10 from 3 game. Ja'Kobe Walter can shoot it too and is quietly turning into a dependable heavy-minute wing.

With a win, Detroit could be in first or second in the East Group A division. The Orlando Magic (2-0) take on the struggling Brooklyn Nets (0-1) tonight. Should Orlando snag a win, they stay atop the group.

One game and one week at a time for Detroit in this tournament. They smacked around the Nets in their first cup game and look to do the same against the Raptors.

#2778. Shane Steichen: Daniel Jones didn't ask to be released

The Colts abruptly released quarterback Daniel Jones on Friday. When coach Shane Steichen spoke to reporters on Friday, he was asked whether Jones asked to be cut.

“No, this was a decision that was just made for both, you know, the best interests of both parties,” Steichen said, via James Boyd of The Athletic.

Steichen also explained the timing by saying, “It’s just where we’re at in our season. . . . That’s just the situation that we’re at right now.”

Steichen also said that, as expected, Anthony Richardson will become the starter.

So instead of squatting on Jones and not letting him play, Jones gets a chance to land with a contender as a backup. Likely on the practice squad, which would give him the ability to jump to an active roster if/when a starter gets injured.

Yahoo Sports is giving fans another way to play fantasy basketball with Perfect 5, a free-to-play game featuring each week's NBA on Prime doubleheader. The rules are simple: pick five players, stay within a $15 budget and rack up fantasy points through scoring, rebounds, assists, defensive stats and 3s.

Friday's slate features the Raptors at Pistons (7:30 p.m. ET) and Rockets at Nuggets (10 p.m. ET), both games NBA Cup Group Play matchups. The injury report is doing most of the talking this week. Cade Cunningham, Alperen Şengün and Scottie Barnes are all questionable, and Detroit is already without Jalen Duren and Duncan Robinson. The Raptors won't have RJ Barrett and Collin Murray-Boyles.

Using Yahoo projections, each player's last five games, the betting lines and the latest injury news, I ran 20,000 simulations of the slate against a simulated Yahoo field built from this week's pick rates. I'm paying up for the best player on the board and filling in around him with $2 and $3 players whose roles just got bigger. Here's my lineup:

This group finished in the top 1% of the simulated field 16.9% of the time — the best rate of the 20,000 lineups I tested — and beat every entry in the field more often than any other build (1.04%). Only about 0.03% of the field has these exact five.

Jokić leads the slate at 54.00 projected fantasy points, more than three points clear of anyone else, on a line of 24.1 points, 10.7 rebounds, 8.9 assists, 1.7 steals and a block. I like the situational spot: Denver is a 3.5-point home favorite, and the 227.5 total is the highest on the slate. Yes, three-quarters of the field has him, but the matchup sets up well, too.

Şengün took a shot to the face in Wednesday's win over Indiana and didn't return. Ime Udoka said he has swelling in his right eye and a scratched cornea in his left. Fading Jokić is a real option in a top-heavy contest like this (see the contrarian build below), but my sims say he's worth going chalk.

Jenkins is the best value on the board and I like him whether Cunningham plays or not. He's projected for 33.02 fantasy points at $3, ahead of several $4 players. He's been hot this week, too: 25 points, 5 rebounds and 5 assists in Tuesday's win over San Antonio, then 17 points and 9 assists as the starting point guard in Wednesday's win at New Orleans. Cunningham sat Wednesday with right knee soreness on the second night of a back-to-back, and he's questionable again Friday. The expectation is he plays. But if he sits, Jenkins runs the offense and his outlook gets even better. That built-in insurance is why he showed up in the single best lineup in nearly 47% of my sims, more than any other player on the slate.

This is my leverage play. Walter is averaging 12.2 points, 2.5 3s and 1.3 steals, and he's projected for 27.15 fantasy points. What makes him interesting is everyone around him. Leonard and Barrett are out and Barnes is questionable after Toronto held him out of the back half of its back-to-back to manage his groin. Murray-Boyles is also in concussion protocol and won't play.

Walter dropped 25 points with seven 3s against the Knicks on Tuesday, then followed it with 18 points, 7 rebounds, 6 assists and 3 steals against Washington. Toronto has lost six straight. Someone has to take shots, and he's shown he will. At 4% picked, he's the piece that separates this lineup from the field.

Huerter was in the single best lineup in 45.3% of my simulations, second only to Jenkins. He's projected for 24.15 fantasy points at $2, and his role is growing with Detroit this banged-up. Johnson is the second-most popular pick in my lineup. He's projected for 23.13 fantasy points at $2, starting next to Jokić in the slate's highest-scoring game. You don't get leverage from him, but you get it from Walter and Jenkins, and that's enough. I'm banking on a bounce-back from the 15.9 fantasy points he scored in 31 minutes versus Houston on Nov. 9.

Using Yahoo's projections, the highest-scoring possible lineup is Jokić, Cunningham, Huerter, Johnson and Alijah Martin at 161.63 fantasy points. Mine comes in just 0.18 points behind it.

On paper, it's the max. In the sims, it finished in the top 1% only 6.6% of the time, less than half the rate of my lineup. Two things hurt it. First, Cunningham's knee: a questionable tag means there's a real chance he sits. Second, Martin is a $1 punt projected under 10 points, so you're leaning on two players to carry the build. Swapping Cunningham and Martin for Jenkins and Walter gives up 0.18 projected points and removes most of that risk.

#2774. Patriots QB Drake Maye reportedly has fractured right fibula, could return later this season

Following testing, New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye reportedly suffered a fractured right fibula in Week 10, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter and Mike Reiss.

Maye will not require surgery and there is a small chance he could be back for the Patriots late in the regular season if they are contending for an AFC playoff spot.

Maye sustained the injury during the team's 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions on Sunday. It happened on the team's first drive, which ended after Maye was sacked by Lions star Aidan Hutchinson.

Maye's injury actually wasn't the focus initially. Following the sack, Hutchinson sustained a torn ACL while celebrating the play. He'll miss the rest of the season due to the injury.

The true extent of Maye's injury came to light on the Patriots' next offensive drive. Backup Tommy DeVito entered the game in place of Maye, who was spotted on the broadcast walking back to the team's locker room. Maye was unable to return to the game, and the team was tight-lipped about the nature of the injury.

Later Sunday, reports started to emerge suggesting Maye could miss "a while." Those reports received more clarity Monday, when it was revealed Maye remained in Germany to receive further evaluation. By Monday morning, it was reported the Patriots feared Maye was dealing with a "significant lower leg injury," possibly a fracture.

The injury could end Maye's third NFL season prematurely. While the 24-year-old got off to a tough start, turning the ball over seven times in the team's first three games, he proved last year's excellence was not a fluke. In the six games leading up to Week 10, Maye had 17 passing touchdowns against five interceptions. He was on pace for yet another strong year before the injury.

While Maye's long-term outlook remains strong, the Patriots' short-term outlook appears disastrous. Following the team's loss in Week 10, the Patriots sit at 5-5 through 10 games. The playoffs are still very much in the picture, but only if the team can rally around its new quarterback. That didn't happen in Week 10, as the team looked listless with DeVito under center.

But DeVito will have the bye week to get fully up to speed. When the Patriots return to action, they'll take on the 1-8 Los Angeles Chargers, giving DeVito an opportunity for a big game in his first start.

After that, though, things get much harder for the Patriots. During the last six weeks of the regular season, New England will take on the Buffalo Bills, Minnesota Vikings, Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos. The team very likely needs to win at least two, possibly three of those games to secure a spot in the postseason.

Getting that done without Maye will be extremely difficult.

#2770. Previewing UVA Football’s home finale versus North Carolina

The past few seasons have seen Tony Elliott repeatedly mention the month of November as time where teams separate themselves from pack. Of course, in the context of this season for the Virginia Cavaliers, that doesn't mean separating for a chance to play for an ACC title, but it could mean salvaging what's left of a season where the results have fallen well short of preseason expectations by going unbeaten in November.

This Saturday is the first of two massive opportunities that will heavily dictate how this season and program as a whole are viewed going forward. Two weeks, two rivalries, against two struggling teams that look much less intimidating than they did two or three weeks ago.

And if you were thinking Tony Elliott was one of those coaches who downplays the significance of rivalry games when he stepped in front of a microphone ahead of this two-game stretch, you would be wrong. In one of the better answers he's given as UVA's head coach, Elliott was asked about what rivalries mean to him even at a time when player movement has never been more hectic:

North Carolina enters this game with a 5-5 overall record of its own and 2-4 mark in the ACC. Bill Belichick's and co. have dropped two of their last three games, including an ugly 16-14 loss at home versus Louisville a week ago.

One way or another, someone is destined to earn a bowl bid on Saturday. Kickoff is set for 12:30 on the CW and here are three players, two keys to the game, and a predication.

Edwards Jr. remains questionable for Saturday after leaving last week's game against Louisville early in the third quarter. We won't know for sure until that first drive, but for a Bill Belichick-coached team, the idea that Edwards Jr. won't be playing in this game could easily be one giant facade.

On the field, Edwards Jr. has had a solid year with the Tar Heels. His best performance came on Halloween in an upset bid that fell just short against Miami, where he went 28-for-34 through the air for 341 yards and four touchdowns. He's tossed for over 2,200 yards on the season to go with 18 touchdowns and six picks on the season.

Interestingly, there's an alternate world where Edwards Jr. is taking snaps for the Cavaliers this weekend. Two Decembers ago, Edwards hit the transfer portal after starting his career at Maryland and was on a visit at UVA the same day Chandler Morris wound up committing to Tony Elliott and the 'Hoos. He enrolled at Wisconsin not long after, where he played in just two games due to a knee injury, then wound up back in the portal and eventually to Chapel Hill.

One of the bigger stories heading into this game revolves around Smith III and the suspension he'll be serving as a result of the scuffle at the end of that Louisville game. Smith III will be out for the first half of Saturday's game, which comes as a big break for UVA's passing game. Not only does Smith III lead his team with three interceptions, he also owns the fourth-most tackles on this Carolina team. The 'Hoos put up 424 total yards of offense against Cal last week, 223 of which came through the air. You would hope Beau Pribula and the receivers could find a way to take advantage of his absence for at least those 30 minutes.

No matter who is taking the snaps at QB, Thurman will be a huge factor in how UNC's offense fares. He's firmly second on this UNC team in catches with 50 and has hauled in eight touchdowns as a reliable safety blanket for Edwards Jr. at 6-foot-6, 245 pounds. He'll by far be the best athlete the 'Hoos have seen this year at the tight end spot. Thurman's well on his way to playing on Monday's, Thursday's, and Sunday's in the near future. He looks more like a receiver than a tight end once he catches the ball and gets downhill.

The 'Hoos were great at forcing Cal to play one-dimensional offense with how they played the run. UNC comes in averaging 114 yards per game on the ground, a mark that's 122nd in the country through their 10 games. They have a handful of guys in Benjamin Hall and Demon June who have shown flashes despite that statistical ranking. UVA will need to keep that rushing number low for a second-straight week, any potential sack yardage aside, without the likes of Landon Danley and Maddox Marcellus out there once again.

Based on the availability report, it appears Caleb Hardy will be back to add a dose of experience alongside Kam Robinson and as another body to slot into the linebacker rotation with Myles Brown and Justin Rowe.

It didn't accumulate to 40 points or anything extraordinary last week, but I thought it was one of the few games this season where the offense looked the way it was built to in terms of how they attacked Cal. 22 offensive points went up on the scoreboard thanks to Beau Pribula making things happen with his legs when needed for 67 yards, coupled with 223 yards of passing offense between both he and Eli Holstein. Four different running backs had 20 or more rushing yards and when Pribula needed short, reliable yards against pressure, Jekail Middlebrook was there to bail him out as a checkdown.

It wasn't the most attractive brand of offense, but those methodical drives for scores gave a glimpse into what this group can do when dialed in. The Tar Heels are average defensively from a yardage perspective. They're in the eighties in rushing and passing yards allowed and are second-worst in the ACC at getting off the field on third down. We simply shouldn't see the 'Hoos sputter on offense in the ways they did against the likes of SMU, Duke, and Wake Forest in this game, but can they take a bigger step forward against a Carolina team that has the athletes to punish Pribula and the offensive line if things aren't buttoned up?

UVA is 5-1 at home this season and 0-4 in games outside of Scott Stadium. It's a jarring split, especially looking ahead to next week. For now, the 'Hoos sit as a 1.5-point favorite; essentially a pick 'em with respect to this game being in Charlottesville.

UVA's pass rush found ways to stifle Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele all game long, totaling four sacks from four different contributors. UNC has allowed at least one sack in all 10 of its games this season. They've given up three or more in five of those. Talk about good timing for this UVA defense.

This is another big oppurtunity for UVA to dictate the terms of the game through their time of possession. It's unlikely we see UNC produce enough on the ground to be able to lean on its running backs 60 minutes and their offensive line has its inconsistencies as well. They'll likely have to throw the ball to win here, meaning another good pass-rush performance would be big in putting UNC in more predictable passing downs behind the sticks to disarm their offense and get the ball back to Pribula to chew additional clock.

I feel weirdly confident in UVA in this spot overall. It would have been so easy to come and look flat last week on a three-game losing streak late in the season. This team clearly still cares, no matter how bad we think Cal really is. These games in November are about who wants it more and it appears UVA still has the right mindset. I'm on this team getting its sixth win here by a healthy seven points.

#2769. Darius Acuff is showing flashes of NBA stardom, but he has one massive problem

Flip on a Sacramento Kings broadcast and you're likely to be inundated with graphics, statistical queries or fun facts framing Darius Acuff Jr. in an illustrious ensemble.

Names like Michael Jordan, LeBron James, Oscar Robertson and Luka Dončić are frequently mentioned alongside the rookie guard, who is averaging a robust 26.2 points, seven assists (3.9 turnovers) and 3.6 rebounds through the first 14 games of his career. It's an esteemed neighborhood for Acuff to reside in and certainly an encouraging omen as he progresses further into his NBA tenure.

Skeptics, however, will peek beyond the box score and point to Sacramento's 1-13 record, Acuff's relative scoring inefficiency (53.3% true shooting, 24th percentile, per Dunks & Threes) or his ball-dominant tendencies to downplay his raw production. They'll note how much of the Kings' 27th-ranked offense is channeled through him and posit his true impact pales in comparison to those All-Star-level statlines by citing a host of metrics and data.

Stretching back to his sensational freshman season at Arkansas a year ago, Acuff has divided the masses with his play. The first month of his rookie campaign has done little to assuage that polarization, a reality existing independent of anything he's responsible for but rather captures the cantankerous discourse enveloping the sports world more than ever these days.

Nonetheless, there is plenty to examine, praise and critique about Acuff's first 14 games. He's flashed loads of promise and indicated various areas of concern as the Kings presumably build around him moving forward. So, what about his skill-set may suggest future stardom and what may offer reasons for worry in an NBA ecosystem increasingly cruel and unforgiving to smaller guards?

Every star player needs a superpower. Some are more consequential or prominent than others but they all have one. Though not a star at this stage, Acuff's superpower is his ability to maintain a live dribble wherever and whenever he desires. That may sound rudimentary. There are a horde of guards who can haphazardly dribble the air out of the ball. But Acuff makes it immensely practical.

As the league continues to evolve and grow sharper fangs defensively while also upsizing its offensive hubs, dribbling — especially inside the arc or against pressure — is a bit of a lost art. So many players are unable to initiate offense while enduring full-court physicality or slalom through gap help. Acuff can.

He's already one of the most dextrous dribblers in the NBA, equipped to prime screens however necessary, vary the height of his dribble to best suit his intentions at any given moment, wind through treacherous limbs and preserve his handle in the face of point-of-attack pestering. If he wants to avoid stunting defenders or insulate the ball from pressure, he'll keep it low. If it's time to rise for a jumper or make a delivery, he pounds the rock to speed up its arrival into his shooting/passing pocket. The toggling between them is seamless, too.

Acuff is not solely a modern Curly Neal, he also touts an incredibly elastic upper body. Such a trait is evident in his dexterity — he can dribble and pass from a variety of arm and hand placements — but spans beyond it, too.

It empowers him to duck low underneath stiffer defenders or coil around them to find opportunistic angles. The dude gyrates, and it's integral to his offensive signature. Any potential stardom will hinge, in part, on his rare intersection of ball-handling and upper-body flexibility that fuels his playmaking and bucket-getting.

That superpower grants Acuff access to virtually any part of the court. The broader the scope a player can access on the court offensively, the better. It renders him a grander threat to defenses as a scorer and passer. Yet right now, Acuff is not an omnipresent threat. His wondrous ball-handling unlocks doors for him he cannot utilize.

He lacks the burst and vertical explosion to create separation as a driver or aptly elevate as a finisher, issues borne through insufficient lower-body strength that prevent him from generating force downhill or through the air.

He is not an imposing scorer around the rim, consistently reduced to attempts well below the basket or unable to discard help inside, even if momentum is in his corner. His handle and upper-body pliability mitigate some of these troubles but not all of them, which rear their head enough to disrupt his game and narrow the avenues where he's a daunting offensive conductor.

According to Cleaning the Glass, 17% of his field goal attempts occur at the rim (30th percentile among point guards) while he's converting just 58% of those attempts (35th percentile). Similarly, he's currently unable to overwhelm defenders and reliably draw fouls. Despite touting the league's sixth-highest usage rate (34.7%) and having taken the third-most shots, he's 39th in free throws attempted (68).

Just look how groundbound he is on these drives, missing both the pop to ease his finishes or the ferocity to challenge bigs inside:

A lean diet of shots at the rim and charity stripe makes for a tough life in building an efficient scoring repertoire. Until or if Acuff adds significant lower-body strength (and gradual increments could facilitate this, it's not all or nothing), the path toward efficient high-volume scorer is to embrace the 3-ball.

He's already doing so off the bounce, launching the league's third-most pull-up triples per game at 6.9. Although he's only netting 32% of those, it's clearly a shot he's hunting and cozying up with, largely against drop coverage around Domantas Sabonis' bludgeoning screens. But he'll also dance into them over switches and still hoist when a trailing point-of-attack defender is re-entering the play.

Thirty-two percent cannot suffice long-term but it's far from a disastrous launching pad. As he approaches his prime, it's entirely plausible the newly minted 20-year-old levels up as a shotmaker to better suit the volume with which he's evidently found comfort.

If Acuff ascends to a requisite level as a long-range pull-up shooter that warps defenses into dissuading those looks, it should benefit his interior pursuits. Deep drop coverage is an arduous tactic for him to attack inside because of aforementioned physical limitations. But seeing more bigs switch or play around the level — and away from the paint — could allow him to weaponize his handle and flexibility into drives without the fear of a rim protector lurking.

Ideally, the Kings will also add another bona fide creator alongside Acuff, whose off-ball game has yet to be spotlighted much because of the rickety ball-handling carousel surrounding him. Among starting guards, his 49.8% on-ball rate ranks third behind Jalen Brunson and Andrew Nembhard, the latter of whom has played much of the year without Tyrese Haliburton (per databallr).

In the rare moments he's been afforded to operate off the ball, his instincts locating space, traversing screens or curling into dribble handoffs lend credence to the notion his sprawling ball dominance is a product of Sacramento's cumbersome infrastructure more than his individual nature.

Even in the small sample he's shared the floor with Malik Monk — who's struggled mightily this year but is still the Kings' most viable non-Acuff creator as someone who can dribble, initiate possessions and operate a ball-screen — Acuff's efficiency spikes without suppressing his volume. Whether it's spotting up, being deployed as a screener or piercing a tilted defense, he's yielded the rewards of defenses fixating on someone else.

Through 14 games, Acuff is shooting 41.7% (15-of-36) on catch-and-shoot threes. An environment promoting more of those chances and opportunities for his quick-witted, malleable decision-making — Acuff adapts his shooting and passing processes on the fly quite well — would simplify his responsibilities without dimming his light.

That doesn't mean Acuff is ill-suited for an on-ball role, he's exhibited reasons to believe in him there. But the extent to which Sacramento relies upon him for it seems detrimental to himself and the collective offense.

Between occasional minutes next to Monk and his screening/handoff camaraderie with Sabonis, the Kings do present a few helping hands for their rookie point guard. That all evaporates defensively, though. There's hardly any safety net.

They're a horrendous rim protection team; opponents shoot a league-high 75.6% at the basket against them, per Cleaning the Glass. They don't have established point-of-attack stoppers or slippery screen navigators. They switch the majority of actions 1-4 because most of their rotation players cannot fight around picks and that makes Acuff a moving target for opposing offenses.

Despite a litany of debilitating factors, Acuff does himself no favors either. He is, thus far, a very, very poor defender. He applies scant physicality on the ball, gets trapped in screens like a never-ending maze, hardly ever forces turnovers or grabs rebounds and is often ill-positioned off the ball without the tools to recover punctually.

Habits like these gleaned from the eye test are reinforced by various datapoints. Per Cleaning the Glass, with Acuff on the floor, opponents take 6.9% more of their shots at the rim, log a 2.1% higher offensive rebounding rate and turn the ball over 3.6% less of the time. His STOP% (steals, blocks recovered, offensive fouls drawn per 100 possessions) is 1.6 and ranks in the 6th percentile, according to databallr.

Playing for the league's 30th-ranked defense exacerbates the magnitude of Acuff's woes but he is culpable for the vast majority of his shortcomings and must improve in the coming years. He does not make offenses feel his presence and appears to simply drift through possessions instead of committing to sustainable defensive efforts.

As defensive-minded players blossom into loftier offensive duties, we sometimes see them regress defensively. Maybe, through an optimistic lens, the opposite can unfold for Acuff. He shoulders a titanic offensive load and has displayed the capacity to function off the ball in a lower-stress role.

For that to ignite meaningful defensive growth, though, Acuff probably has to infuse substantial lower-body strength. It'll make him sturdier and more liable to anchor against contact, which he's mostly shied away from altogether, and accelerate his lateral mobility, where he concedes breakdowns because he cannot slide quickly enough to cut off ball-handlers.

Achieving this could address glaring limitations on both sides of the ball and amplify his superpowers — the very ones propelling him into graphics of glory alongside Hall of Famers. Maybe someday, Acuff, too, will be the sort of complimentary company rookie guards hope to join if they burst onto the NBA scene.

#2767. How the 49ers are uniquely equipped to beat the Vikings

The Week 11 NFL slate leaves a lot to be desired. Two games on the schedule involve playoff teams. The big one is an international outing between the Minnesota Vikings and the San Francisco 49ers.

The Vikings saw their season circling the drain, so they went out and traded for a familiar face in Kirk Cousins. Nobody was happier with the trade than Justin Jefferson, who caught a season-high nine passes in Cousins' debut last week.

Missed opportunities defined Raheem Morris's stop unit last week, as he explained. The Niners defense will look to bounce back after a game in which they finished in the 6th percentile in points allowed per drive.

The other side of the ball features two of the very best at what they do. The mad scientist Brian Flores boasts one of the most impressive defenses we've seen through 10 weeks. Minnesota bottled up a high-powered Lions offense, kept the Bills in check, and turned Jordan Love and the Packers offense into a pumpkin last week.

The only team to slow down the 49ers offense this year is themselves. They've surpassed 30 points five times this season, including a season-high 46 points last week against the Cowboys. Big plays were the name of the game for San Francisco, as they were in the 99th percentile in EPA per play against Dallas.

The biggest edge in this game is on special teams. Minnesota ranks first in schedule-adjusted efficiency, while the Niners rank 29th. The Vikings are fifth or better in field goals, kickoff return, punt return, and are sixth in hidden points.

The 49ers are smack dab in the middle at 16th in hidden points, largely because of their punter. But it shouldn't surprise anyone to see the punt return unit rank second-to-last, or the field goal team come in at 28th. The third phase of the game is generally what decides these one-possession contests.

Let's dig deeper into each offense and defense to see how this game could play out.

Contrary to what you might have seen online leading up to this game, the 49ers defense and Vikings offense do exist. Flores and Shanahan are not the only play-callers in this game.

The Vikings scored 30 against the Packers, so the initial thought might be that Kirk Cousins was all that was needed to jumpstart an offense that has been dormant all year.

After going three-and-out and losing a yard to begin the game, the Vikings had a drive that started on Green Bay's 10-yard line. They lost six yards and had to settle for a field goal.

On the next drive, the Vikings had another short field after the Packers missed a field goal. Myles Price caught a 38-yard touchdown on 3rd and 23 on a play that should have never resulted in a completion.

After going three-and-out on their ensuing drive, Cousins threw an interception in the red zone, but his knee was down. On 3rd and 15, Green bay was in press man coverage with no safety help, and gave up 24 yards. Minnesota scored on the next play.

Thirty points. One drive that was legit. Zooming out, the Vikings had an EPA per play in the 54th percentile, a success rate in the 52nd percentile, and a yards per play in the 28th percentile. Cousins was money on third downs, which flipped the variance in the Vikings favor.

Functionally, the Vikings struggle to run the rock. Minnesota is running more gap and man concepts than ever under Kevin O'Connell, which may explain some of the struggles. Despite ranking fifth in the league in yards before contact, Minnesota is 25th in rushing success rate and 29th in EPA per rush.

They had a 12-yard run last week on a pitch to a wide reciever. Aaron Jones shook free from a 19-yarder. But he only averaged 4.3 yards per carry. Their rushing leader, old friend Jordan Mason, had 16 carries, but could only muster 3.7 yards per carry.

It's easy to chalk up a subpar run game to poor quarterback play, but the Vikings are 27th in team rush yards over expectation at -73, and are 21st in 10+ yard rushes.

I've always appreciated Mason for being a tough, hard-nosed runner. What the Niners do well is exactly how you keep Mason under wraps. All the slanting and stunting the defensive line does will force Mason to redirect. That's what you want. If you let Mason pick up some steam, he'll pick up 5-7 yards, easily. But if you make him change directions, he turns into a medicore back.

It's tough to use 5-down fronts against a wide open offense like the Cowboys, who live three wide receiver sets. Minnesota uses 11 personnel nearly 40% less than Dallas. O'Connell uses two tight end sets 27.7% of the time, which is the 9th highest-rate in the league, and runs plays from under center at the sixth-highest clip.

Against 5-down fronts last week, the Vikings had 15 carries and averaged 3.8 yards. I'd expect Raheem Morris to deploy more 5-down fronts than usual, especially on early downs, to keep the Vikings in longer down and distances. It also means more Jaden Dugger, which is a good thing, who only played 11 snaps last week.

Something smells about the Vikings run game. The 49ers have to win this facet of the game. The defense has allowed five rushes of 10+ yards this season, far and away the best in the league (second place has allowed 16).

They're second in rushing EPA on the season. Minnesota's offensive line is far from a bully ball unit. Their tight ends aren't effective in the run game, which could lead to multiple negatives to force obvious passing downs. They ask 180-pound receivers to block in the fit, and the results are as you'd imagine. This is the type of game where you notice Nick Bosa and Mykel Williams control the line of scrimmage.

Christmas came early for Justin Jefferson last week. He saw a season-high 13 targets. Kyler Murray acts like it's against the rules to throw the ball over the middle of the field, which is why Jefferson only has nine targets in the middle third this season. His 49 yards are tied for 146th in the NFL, per Next Gen Stats. That'll change with Cousins, who has the second-most yards this season over the middle of the field.

The Packers tried to bracket Jefferson at times last week, but to no avail. Credit Cousins for throwing the ball on time before the double team could get there. But the Packers had opportunities for turnovers on Jefferson targets. They dropped an interception.

You'll live with the underneath throws, like the curls and the screens — but you better make a tackle and limit the damage after the catch. What you have to take away are the deep over routes or any kind of crossing route. You're not going to shutdown a focal point of the offense like Jefferson. However, you can eliminate throwing zones schematically and ensure he doesn't beat you over the top.

Fred Warner has erased the middle of the field this entire decade. Teams simply do not target the intermediate part fo the field with No. 54 on the field. Dak Prescott had 51 attempts in Week 10. Six of those were beyond 10 yards over the middle. Warner lurking in that area should impact how the Vikings want to attack San Francisco.

If Price or Felton beat you, then so be it. There isn't a George Pickens at WR2 for Minnesota. The 49ers are much better equipped to slow down this unit than they were last week.

The most impressive part about Brian Flores is his ability to dictate what an offense does. He makes coordinators tuck their tail and get out of what they wnat to do offensively. He speeds quarterbacks up with the blitz, but limits their options since extra blockers have to stay in and pass protect.

Flores' scheme takes immense pressure off his coverage unit, while creating 1-on-1s across the board for his pass rush. It's fascinating to watch.

Last week, the Packers had five elgiible receivers run a route on 33.7% of their dropbacks. It felt like Jordan Love left a few plays on the field, because he either didn't have or wasn't aware of where his outlet was when the pressure got to him.

If we reference the teams since the Vikings bye, the Colts used five eligibles on 25.9 percent of their plays, the Lions were at 24.1%, while the Bills were at 47.2%.

The team that used the most eligbles at the highest clip scored the most against the Vikings, you say? Per Sumer Sports, Brock Purdy has 298 dropbacks this season. The 49ers have used five eligible receivers run a route on 239 of those dropbacks. That's good for a league-high 80.2% of the time.

Against Minnesota, you have to fight pressure with pressure. You're going to take your fair share of licks. But if you can withstand enough jabs and avoid the haymakers, you can land a few of your own.

One way to do that is by getting all of your eligibles in a route. For the 49ers, that's simply running their offense. Buffalo turned quick play-action and screen passes into a profit. Quick dump-offs to tight ends for eight yard gains are big wins against this defense.

To me, if you're an EPA(big play) team, like the Packers, the Vikings are the worst-possible matchup. Whereas a success rate driven offense, like the 49ers, can thrive against Minnesota. Love has been conditioned, by way of his offense, to hunt the big play. Brock Purdy is undoubtedly as aggressive, but there are far more built-in outs at every level in a Kyle Shanahan offense than there are a Matt LaFleur offense.

Green Bay had several plays where Dallas Turner or Andrew Van Ginkel were in a bind in coverage, but they couldn't take advantage. Instead, Love was sacked because his eyes were downfield.

Those will show up this week with Christian McCaffrey 1-on-1 in the open field, or Keenan Allen settling into the vacated area of a blitzer, or George Kittle and Deebo Samuel keeping the offense ahead of the chains on a screen pass.

There's no need to inundate you with numbers about the Vikings offense. They're excellent. They're the best in the league in EPA per play, success rate, points per drive allowed, and third in schedule-adjusted efficiency. But for as much of a step up in class as this is for the Niners offense, the same is true for Flores and company.

Mike Evans is expected to play. They have not seen a No. 1 receiver in the same stratosphere as Evans. The Bills are an elite running team, but that is a choppy passing game short on weapons. The Lions are the closest passing attack to the 49ers, but one quarterback thrives under chaos, while the other has cement feet and can't get himself out of trouble.

In the same way Dallas was uniquely equipped to harrass the Niners defense, I feel the same way this week with this iteration of Shanahan's offense going up against Flores. Purdy knows the offense inside and out. We've seen him get to the third and fourth progressions, scramble for first downs when nothing is there, or maniuplate space in the pocket to help buy time for his wideouts.

It felt like it had been a few weeks since we saw the 49ers run a screen. That changed last week. This season, the Vikings have faced 17 screen passes. They're allowing 8.59 yards per play with a 64.7% success rate. That'll be a key cog for the Niners this week, especially to help slow the pass rush of Minnesota down.

There will be sacks. There might be turnovers. But it's not a game where Connor Colby should be overwhelmed. There is no Quinnen Williams for him to go against. Minnesota's defensive tackles are more of the stout variety, which are not the kinds that give Colby issues.

Dallas Turner exclusively lines up on the edge. If the ball is on the hash, that's where Turner will line up. So, there won't be any guessing games as to where Turner will be. You cannot say the same about who is coming. Purdy can expect as many as six players around the line of scrimmage and won't know which player is blitzing until the ball is snapped.

The Vikings are the only team in the league with a double-digit sack percentage. They get pressure on nearly half of their dropbacks, and only one team generates quicker pressure than Minnesota. There are two sides to every coin, though. Brock Purdy has been pressured the third-least of any quarterback and, even after last week, is still the third-least sacked quarterback in the league.

There are free access throws outside of the numbers for the taking that teams have shied away from. Whether it's something the 49ers look to exploit early on in the game or in the second half, it's another area where this team, unlike the others Minnesota has faced, can lean on to stay ahead of the chains and into managable third downs.

Good luck running the ball on this defense. Minnesota is sixth in EPA per rush, but are stingy on a down-to-down basis, ranking third in success rate.

It's difficult to generate any zone concepts, since the majority of defenders are at the line of scrimmage. It's all 1-on-1s, nobody can climb to the second level, and it's a jumbled mess at the line of scrimmage.

It'll be interesting to see if Shanahan uses more draw concepts. That's not something the Vikings have seen much. Counter plays haven't found much daylight. Since Week 7, Minnesota allows a 21.4% success rate and only 2.93 yards per carry.

There is one run concept where teams have found success against Flores's defense. That's running power. During that same stretch, it's the one play you can get over on the Vikings defense.

Skol fans found that tweet and chalked those runs up to being late in the game when the Vikings defense was tired. Try again. The Packers had an 11-yard gain in the first quarter running power last week. They did not run it again until the third quarter. The Bills had a pair of 7-yard gains in the second quarter. The Lions had an 8-yard gain in the first quarter.

Power has been the 49ers go-to run in short-yardage and goalline situations this season, which is why they lead the league with a 55.6% success rate. To me, you run the ball against the Vikings to stay out of third-and-oh no. That's when Flores gets you. Those downs are where your offenses go to die.

The Colts had 33 carries for 154 yards. The Lions ran for 230 yards. The Bills had 44 carries. Buffalo only averaged three yards per carry, but they stayed on the field.

Shanahan has to be willing to run the ball on third down. That's when you can gash the Vikings. While that's a possibility, the goal should be to wear them down, stay on the field, and make a unit that's closer to a sum of its parts than a star-studded one…play football.

The Niners have the upper-hand at the skill positions. They're not going to score 40 points, but picking them to score fewer than 23 is something that we will do once we see it happen.

In a game between two potential NFC squads battling for playoff positioning, we'll take the team that resembles what a contender looks like. The Vikings will make it tough, but there will be some late separation as the Niners offense will be too much when it's all said and done.

#2764. Adam Schefter shares major injury updates on Drake Maye and A.J. Brown

The New England Patriots got long-awaited news on their two injured stars, quarterback Drake Maye and wide receiver A.J. Brown.

According to ESPN's Adam Schefter and Mike Reiss, Maye suffered a fractured right fibula in last week's game against the Detroit Lions. The injury occurred during the first drive of the game when the third-year quarterback was sacked by Lions star edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson.

Per the report, Maye will not need surgery, and there was no additional ligament damage. That leaves open the possibility that he could return "toward the end of the season" if the Patriots are still competing for a playoff spot.

"There was no additional ligament damage, sources told ESPN, which leaves open the possibility, but hardly a certainty, that Maye could return toward the end of the season if New England is in playoff contention."

As for Brown, the three-time All-Pro wide receiver went down with a hamstring injury against the Lions. He is reportedly expected to be sidelined for multiple weeks with the injury.

It's a tough blow for the Patriots to lose both Maye and Brown during a potential playoff run. The team is currently sitting at 5-5 with a legitimate shot at sneaking in as a wild card.

They still have three seemingly winnable games against the Los Angeles Chargers, Miami Dolphins and New York Jets. However, the other four games left on the schedule will be a murderer's row slate against the Minnesota Vikings, Buffalo Bills, Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos.

For now, there are expected to roll with their backup quarterback, Tommy DeVito, moving forward.

#2762. Anthony Richardson gets final Colts’ chance after ominous NFL evaluation

This may be Anthony Richardson's final chance to impress both the Colts and NFL.

Following Indianapolis' stunning decision to release Daniel Jones on Friday, Richardson has been named the starter beginning in Week 12 against the Giants.

This six-game audition is notable since longtime Colts reporter Bob Kravitz reported Thursday night that the Colts have tried to trade the former first-round pick, but "nobody was interested."

Indianapolis Colts quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr. (5) walks off the field against the Houston Texans on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, at Reliant Stadium. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Richardson now has up to five games — vs. Giants, at Eagles, at Titans, vs. Bengals, at Browns and vs. Jaguars — to prove his worth before he becomes a free agent at season's end.

A good showing could, in theory, help him land a contract, perhaps with the Colts or a quarterback-needy team instead of being viewed as a potential practice-squad option.

Richardson will at least have the chance to change his team's opinion after it seemed he couldn't get off the bench no matter how bad Jones played.

Plenty wondered why the Colts had not benched Jones in a lost 3-8 season and the their resistance did not speak well on the former Florida star.

Once viewed as the franchise cornerstone after being selected No. 4 overall in 2023, Richardson experienced highs and lows while making 15 starts over the 2023 and 2024 seasons.

Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) throws before an NFL football game against the Houston Texans in Houston, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. AP Photo/David J. Phillip

His career seemingly nosedived after he asked out of a game for a play in the 2024 season since he felt tired and he later would be benched for Joe Flacco.

The Colts then signed Jones to be their starter and Richardson appeared in just four games over the last two years with no starts.

He appeared in mop-up duty during Thursday's 26-3 road loss to the Texans.

There had been some speculation as to why Richardson didn't replace Jones since the team hesitated to say on the record.

One idea had been that going to Richardson is a move that ends Jones' tenure, and perhaps that was a top consideration since the team did release Jones while clearing the path for Richardson.

The Colts obviously need a long-term quarterback and perhaps he can win them over, although he'll reportedly be looking to change the perception of the 31 other teams, as well.

It's certainly notable that Richardson reportedly didn't draw trade interest since there are many instances of teams taking fliers on early-round flameouts.

The Cowboys traded a fourth-round pick for Trey Lance. The Giants sent the Vikings a fifth-round for J.J. McCarthy. The Jaguars swapped a sixth-rounder for Mac Jones.

Indianapolis Colts quarterbacks Anthony Richardson Sr. (5) and Daniel Jones (17) warm up before a game against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Richardson certainly has similar pedigrees to those other quarterbacks, yet they have received second chances and he's only now getting off the bench after two years.

With a strong showing in these last six games, he may work his way into teams' plans.

#2760. Don’t buy this hype: Why UCLA is in real danger against Michigan

One of the two remaining undefeated big-time college football teams heads into a tough cross-country road trip in Saturday's Week 12 action.

UCLA enters its matchup against Michigan perfect through 10 games, but there are some reasons to question whether the Bruins are as dominant as their record suggests.

Here are three concerns the Big Ten's highest-placed team have going into Michigan.

UCLA averaged 253.2 rushing yards per game and 6.1 yards per carry over its first five games.

Over its last five, those numbers have dropped to 152.2 yards per game and 4.1 yards per carry. That's a significant decline of more than 100 rushing yards per game.

More: Predicting Big Ten football scores in CFB Week 12

Michigan, meanwhile, allows just 103.1 rushing yards per game, and around 3 per carry.

If the Wolverines can take away UCLA's ground game, they can force the Bruins into more predictable passing situations and make life considerably harder for this offense.

Michigan quarterback Tommy Carr (14) runs against Penn State during the second half at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Credit: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Michigan's offense is certainly not without problems. It ranks 131st nationally in total production, averaging just 300.9 yards per game. And it's seventh-worst in FBS in scoring.

Their quarterback situation has been unsettled, and losing leading receiver J.J. Buchanan, who accounted for 646 receiving yards, makes an already struggling passing attack even more concerning.

The Wolverines don't need to suddenly become an offensive powerhouse to threaten UCLA. They need to establish enough of a running game, protect the football, and capitalize on opportunities.

If Michigan's defense can slow UCLA's rushing attack and force Dieffenbach to win through the air, the Wolverines have a realistic opportunity to keep this game close.

More: Bold predictions for CFB's biggest Week 12 games

UCLA is unquestionably the more complete team, but its declining rushing production and Michigan's relative defensive strengths create a matchup worth watching.

An upset isn't the most likely outcome, but it's certainly not out of the question.

The Big Lead prediction: UCLA 23, Michigan 19

#2758. NBA trade rumors 2026-27: Dejounte Murray update (or, non-update), Kyrie Irving, Trey Murphy, more

Don't expect any NBA trades before Dec. 15, when many of the players who signed new contracts or extensions this summer become eligible to be traded. Even then, it's more likely we'll get closer to the February trade deadline before we see any notable names moved. That includes the guy in the sub-headline below.

While the insatiable NBA rumor mill keeps trying to find clickable updates on Dejounte Murray trades — "The Pelicans talked to the Suns!!!" — the reality is there is no traction toward any kind of deal for the New Orleans guard. Grant Liffman and Chris Mannix break it down well in the video above, but here is the latest.

• Murray, through his agents at Klutch Sports, made a trade request, and the Pelicans publicly acknowledged that, saying, "We will evaluate potential trade opportunities that are in the best interest of our organization." New Orleans hasn't found that yet. Meanwhile, Murray's body language on the court betrays how unhappy he is, and he is shooting 29.6% from 3-point range this season, which doesn't help his trade value.

• To be blunt, teams around the league view Murray as a negative value contract. Those are hard to trade. The fact he is making $32.8 million this season and has a $30.8 million player option for next season also gives teams pause. He is viewed as a 30-year-old guard who's shot 41.9% overall and 30% from 3 in the last two-plus seasons.

• While Murray's camp seems to continue to push the Suns as a destination, league sources have told NBC Sports the Suns have minimal interest, unless the Pelicans want to attach sweetener, such as a first-round pick. That's been reported a lot of other places as well, it's no secret. While the Suns could use a point guard and have done background work on Murray (according to Brian Windhorst of ESPN), they aren't sold on Murray being the All-Star player he was five years ago, and he hasn't looked the same coming off his torn Achilles. How much interest the Pelicans have in Jalen Green should be another question.

• When teams do call the Pelicans, they are more likely to ask about Trey Murphy III and Herb Jones. But Joe Dumars is keeping the price ridiculously high — the Pelicans turned down a trade that would have netted them at least two first-round picks for Murphy over the summer, Michael Scotto of Hoopshype reports.

• Jake Fischer of The Stein Line reports the Suns are more interested in adding a big man with Mark Williams out for the season.

• Utah is one of the teams giving "internal consideration" a potential Kyrie Irving trade, if (or, more likely when) the Mavericks start listening to offers, reports Ian Begley of SNY.TV.

It's worth noting that teams have internal discussions about a lot of players and deals that they never even bother to reach out to the other team about in a serious manner, and where Irving fits in the young timeline in Utah is a good question, but the rumor is out there.

• Multiple reports have coach Brian Keefe's seat in Washington getting hot. This was a team that made moves for veterans in Anthony Davis (playing well) and Trae Young (not playing well) to try and win now, and with the team off to a 5-11 start, someone may be the scapegoat. Washington should have just pivoted to building around AJ Dybantsa, but they are going to be stuck with that horrible four-year, $212 million extension they gave Young this summer for a while. That is the most untradable contract in the league right now.

• Multiple reports have teams interested in trading for Bulls guard Tre Jones. Here is what Zach Lowe said on his Ringer podcast: "Teams are already calling the Bulls about Tre Jones... if he's not the best backup point guard in the NBA, he's very close. If they trade him, they're gonna get real stuff."

#2756. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2751. Padres' Mason Miller, Blue Jays' Louis Varland named MLB Relievers of the Year in first-ever BBWAA award

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller and Toronto Blue Jays closer Louis Varland have been named the winners of the first-ever Baseball Writers Association of America Reliever of the Year award. The BBWAA introduced the award this year and, moving forward, will hand it out annually along with Rookies and Managers of the Year, Cy Young, and MVPs.

The BBWAA's Reliever of the Year award is separate from the Mariano Rivera Award and Trevor Hoffman Award, which honor the best relievers in the American League and National League, respectively. The Rivera and Hoffman Awards replaced the Delivery Man of the Year Award in 2015 and are voted on by a panel of former relievers, including Rivera and Hoffman.

Like the other BBWAA awards, the new Reliever of the Year award is voted on by BBWAA members (two per MLB city in each league). Votes were submitted before the beginning of the playoffs, meaning that only regular-season contributions are taken into account.

The best closer in baseball is the first-ever BBWAA National League Reliever of the Year. Miller was overwhelming from start to finish this past season, pitching to a 1.67 ERA with 129 strikeouts in only 70 innings. He led all pitchers with 3.9 WAR, well ahead of second-place Louie Varland (3.1 WAR), and he led the NL in saves (38) and games finished (57).

Miller's strikeout rate lapped the field. Here are the highest strikeout rates (strikeouts per batter faced) among qualified relievers:

Miller just completed his first full season with the Padres. He was acquired from the Athletics at the 2025 trade deadline at a very high cost: San Diego sent shortstop Leo De Vries, one of the best prospects in baseball, to the A's in the six-player deal. Miller has been worth the price, though. He owns a 1.45 ERA in parts of two seasons with the Padres.

This is the first major award of Miller's career, who finished fourth in the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year voting and has two All-Star Game selections (2024 and 2026), but otherwise had never received Cy Young or MVP votes prior to this season. He beat out the Brewers' Trevor Megill and Phillies' Jhoan Duran for the award.

After jumping into the national spotlight with his high usage during the 2025 postseason, Varland is the first winner of the BBWAA American League Reliever of the Year award. His 1.27 ERA led qualified relievers and his 3.1 WAR was tops in the AL. Varland struck out 87 batters in 78 innings and was fifth with 35 saves. He won with his sheer dominance, not his saves total.

Varland was a workhorse for the Blue Jays this year, much like he was last October. He finished second in saves of at least four outs during the regular season:

The Blue Jays acquired Varland from the Minnesota Twins, his hometown team, at the 2025 trade deadline. He struggled initially after the deal, posting a 4.94 ERA with Toronto after the deadline, but Varland found his footing in the postseason and then found another gear in 2026. He was one of the game's best relievers and a true workhorse.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski has unanimously been named National League Cy Young Award winner for the 2026 Major League Baseball season. He beat out the Phillies' Cristopher Sánchez and the Braves' Chris Sale.

Misiorowski takes home the honors of the Baseball Writers Association of America vote, which was revealed on Wednesday night. Misiorowski's triumph comes after a stellar age-24 season for the World Series champions:

In addition to the top-line numbers above, Misiorowski struck out 37.9% of opposing batters, which is tops in all of MLB and a sky-scraping figure for any pitcher, let alone a starter. Miz also paced the majors in FIP with a mark of 2.17, and his ERA+ of 232 is the 13th-highest figure by a qualifier ever in MLB. Misiorowski's WAR of 6.4 ranked third in the NL behind Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo of the Philadelphia Phillies.

Misiorowski was perhaps even more notable for his blazing fastball than he was the dominance of his statistical outputs. For the season, Misiorowski averaged 100.6 mph with his heavily used four-seamer, and on multiple occasions during 2026 he threw the fastest pitch on record, including this 105.5 mph offering from June:

105.5 MPH FROM JACOB MISIOROWSKI 🔥🔥 pic.twitter.com/wjvkdc7iWE

While Misiorowski's playoff performance was not part of the Cy Young criteria – ballots are submitted before the playoffs begin – he did post a 1.89 ERA in four starts this postseason for the Brewers, who wound up winning it all for the first time in franchise history.

Misiorowski is now the fourth Brewer to win the Cy Young Award. Corbin Burnes won in 2021, and Pete Vuckovich and Rollie Fingers won in 1982 and 1981, respectively, when the franchise was part of the American League.

Given his level of dominance and relative youth, Misiorowski figures to enter the 2027 season as the odds-on favorite to win the hardware again. If he does, he'll become the first back-to-back Cy Young winner in the NL since Jacob deGrom of the New York Mets in 2018 and 2019.

#2746. Drake Maye injury: Everything we know about the Patriots QB’s status

Their Week 10 game against the Detroit Lions was the worst-case scenario for the New England Patriots. Not only were they blown out with a final score of 35-10 to drop to 5-5 on the season, they also lost their starting quarterback to an injury: Drake Maye exited the game in the first quarter due to what was later announced as an ankle injury.

Shortly after the game, information was scarce but the first bits and pieces have started to come in. Based on everything we know, here is what we can say about Maye and his injury situation.

The Patriots started Sunday's game against the Lions with the ball, and actually moved down the field relatively well; it took them only eight plays to get from their own 25-yard line to the Detroit 3. Once there, however, things started to fall apart.

Two penalties bookending an incomplete pass set up a 3rd-and-goal from the 13-yard line, and that play turned into a disaster for the Patriots. Aidan Hutchinson easily got around left tackle Christian Elliss, and dragged Maye down from behind and he was climbing an increasingly collapsing pocket. Along the way, the two-time Pro Bowl edge came down on Maye's right ankle.

He did get up under his own power, but Maye showed a noticeable limp while making his way toward the sideline. Once there, he received attention from the team's medical staff and afterwards headed into the blue medical tent. When he emerged, still clearly hobbled, backup quarterback Tommy DeVito was already getting ready to enter the game.

Maye slowly walked back to the locker room shortly thereafter, and initially labeled questionable to return by the team. Midway through the second quarter, he was downgraded to out.

Neither head coach Mike Vrabel nor any of his teammates were able to provide an update on Maye's status during their post-game media availability.

"Obviously, he wasn't able to finish the game, so we'll have to get some more tests run and we'll see when we come back what it ends up being and the severity of whatever injury he has," Vrabel said at the podium.

"I know that it was a low leg injury. I don't know the exact details of it but I know he couldn't go back in. … He couldn't function. Couldn't play. Couldn't run. Couldn't do whatever he needed to do to play quarterback, to protect himself, to execute, or function at that level."

Left tackle Will Campbell, who briefly occupied the blue medical tent before Maye went in, gave some more information in the postgame locker room.

"I talked to him," Campbell told MassLive's Mark Daniels. "He's in good spirits and just waiting to hear more information about what it is, and just told him I love him and praying for him and he's going to be fine. He's a fighter. Whatever comes his way, he's going to attack it full head of steam and come back better."

The Patriots will fly back to the United States on Sunday, with some follow-up testing expected to take place after the team's arrival on Monday.

[UPDATE 11/16/2026] Initial reports suggest that Maye suffered a "significant lower leg injury" that might keep him out for the remainder of the season. For the Patriots, this is very much the worst-case scenario.

[UPDATE 11/16/2026] The Patriots are concerned that Maye suffered a fractured ankle against the Lions.

[UPDATE 11/16/2026] Drake Maye did not travel back to the United States with the rest of the Patriots, per head coach Mike Vrabel.

"He'll be traveling back here shortly. Just wanted to make sure that everything was good for him to travel back and safely. The things that go around injuries and just wanted to make sure everything was in line for him to travel, and it seems like he is. He'll be returning here, I think, shortly."

[UPDATE 11/16/2026] If indeed diagnosed as a fractured ankle, Drake Maye would "almost certainly" be out for the rest of the season, according to a report by Ian Rapoport.

[UPDATE 11/17/2026] Appearing on local radio, Patriots safety Kevin Byard said that Maye was "probably out for the season."

[UPDATE 11/19/2026] Speaking to Scott Zolak in a 1-on-1 interview, Mike Vrabel referenced Maye's injury being a "short term" issue: "I think he's going to be unavailable here for the short time, and we'll see how that goes down the road."

[UPDATE 11/20/2026] According to a report by ESPN, Maye suffered a fractured fibula without any ligament damage against the Lions. While no surgery will be necessary, the injury will sideline him deep into the season if not for the remainder of the year.

"Any time your starting quarterback goes out and is not able to return, there are questions," safety Kevin Byard told the media after the game.

The questions mentioned by Byard are manifold in the direct aftermath of both the injury and the contest as a whole. Information about severity or a potential recovery timeline is limited, which in turn also limits the avenues the Patriots might have to explore in the immediate or long-term future.

What we do know is that for however long Maye is sidelined, Tommy DeVito will be the top quarterback on the depth chart with third-stringer Behren Morton backing him up. DeVito completed 12 of 24 pass attempts for 81 yards with one touchdown and interception each after entering the Lions game midway through the first period.

DeVito described his and the offense's performance after he took over for Maye as "not good enough." The next chance to improve upon it will come after the Patriots' upcoming bye, with a Sunday Night game versus the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 12. New England will not start its on-field preparation for that game until a few days beforehand; the team will return to its usual in-game schedule following the bye.

[UPDATE 11/16/2026] If the injury is indeed as significant as believed, here is a rundown of how it would impact the Patriots moving forward.
